I closed this shop in August of 2022 and had some leftover un-sold product. Here it is, brand NEW OLD STOCK, full warranty, only for sale to 48 states continental USA. NO RETURNS /LIMIT 2 PER HOUSEHOLD/ NO TAXES CHARGES / SHIPPING IS INCLUDED IN THE PRICE! About the OCD Born in 2004, The OCD has become one of the most sought after overdrives ever made, a fact born out by the many shitty Chinese-made clones being offered up by large companies too unscrupulous and cheap to license the real deal. They still haven’t got it right. V2 FEATURES: Output Buffer (when pedal is turned on I True-Bypass mode, or always when in Enhanced Bypass mode)) which eliminates it from being influenced be effects that came after it. Translation, your sound remains consistent regardless of placement in today’s more complex signal-chains, loopers, and pedalboards. This buffer also had a positive effect on the sound, it reduced loading on the pedal’s hard-clipping stage, allowing more sustain of both the sound and the overtones. Class A configured discrete 2N5457 JFET input section , raising the input impedance to 1 mega ohms (previously 330K) and increasing the dynamics…resulting in significantly better interaction with both single coil and humbuckers. Internal switch to choose between ”Enhanced Bypass TM ” & True-Bypass, and with no popping sound in either mode. No other company offers EB…I invented it. A downside to True-Bypass: True-Bypass (TB) switching was the ultimate way to achieve a clean signal path for many years. Everything’s different now, most guitarists have elaborate pedalboards with 10 or more pedals being the norm, and tremendous potential for signal and tone loss with the many cables, connectors, and other pedals involved in the chain. There can be so much signal loss that it sounds nothing like the sound of a guitar with a cable straight into the front of a great tube amp. Uninspiring. What’s the pedal industries’ solution to this problem for the last 40 years? Unity-gain buffered bypass…i.e. a couple of Field effect Transistors (FETs) configured as unity-gain buffers ala Boss, Ibanez, etc, etc. What’s the benefit to unity-gain FET buffered bypass? It reduces the loading effect that occurs using long lengths of cable, and you remove the loud “popping” sound when switching the device on and off. What’s the issue with unity-gain FET buffered bypass? Although my ears always told me that it sounded “tinny” and that there was signal loss, with the help of a my favorite Electronic Engineer (using some very expensive test equipment) we recently documented that each unity-gain FET buffer actually cuts the gain somewhere between 0.3 to 0.6 dB. This loss of gain is in the low-Mids and Bass frequencies, resulting in that “tinny” sound now that the highs remained and some of the bass and mids are gone. Now factor in that there are two FETs per pedal required to couple the IN & OUT path, that’s an obvious loss of between 1dB-2dB per pedal. What’s an even bigger issue with this old style unity-gain FET bypass? Show original For those who bought a Fulltone OCDv2 but don't know how to shape their sound | 3 settings to try first 1 ketunemikku 2026年9月20日 17:29 Hello, this is Ketsunemic. Once again, I would like to talk about the "Effector Explanation Sheet" project that I have been steadily working on recently. What I have completed this time is a two-page set for the Fulltone OCDv2. To begin with, why did I decide to summarize this on paper? The trigger was a very common scene. You get an effector, go home, and excitedly open the box. You plug it into an amp and step on the switch. …And then, what happens next? There are three knobs and one small switch. Even though it's just that, you suddenly don't know where or how to turn them. I remember this clearly myself. Starting with "everything at 12 o'clock for now," vaguely turning up the Drive, vaguely tweaking the Tone, and stopping at "well, I guess this is fine." And a few months later, that pedal quietly disappears from the board. This is by no means because the pedal was bad. It's just that no one told me where to place the first step . There is a mountain of information if you search online, but staring at your smartphone while playing is quite a mood killer. Something you can check just by dropping your gaze slightly while holding your guitar. I wish I had something like that at my feet. That thought was the starting point for this series. Page 1: "Sound Creation Guide" — A place to return to when you're lost "Sound Creation Guide." I have summarized the basic settings you want to learn first and the roles of the three knobs. So, here is the first page. There was only one thing I really wanted to convey on this page. VOLUME at 9 o'clock, DRIVE at 10 o'clock, TONE at 12 o'clock, and LP. This is the starting point for creating your sound with the OCDv2. It is not the correct answer. It is simply a starting point where "it's hard to get lost if you start here." On the top half of the page, I placed the roles of each of the three knobs along with an illustration of the unit itself. VOLUME is the output level. Let's try starting from a low position, I say. DRIVE is the amount of distortion. The more you turn it to the right, the more the distortion increases, I say. TONE is the brightness of the high-frequency range. Turning it to the right strengthens the highs, I say. And on the bottom right is the HP/LP toggle switch. I wrote, "Try LP first, and if you want to increase the distortion, compare it by listening to HP." For those who thought, "Isn't that obvious?" You are absolutely right. But I believe there is meaning in having this obvious information at hand in a form you can follow with your eyes while playing. On the bottom half, I prepared a section called "Do you have these concerns?" How far should I turn up the distortion? Are the highs too strong? Does the volume change when turned ON? These three are paths I have walked hundreds of times myself. For each, I briefly indicated only where to move: "Adjust VOLUME from a low position when the volume is different," "Move DRIVE little by little when comparing distortion," and "Move TONE little by little when the brightness bothers you." I haven't written the answers. Because the answers only exist in your room, with your amp, and in your ears. All I can do is point to where you should reach out. Page 2: "Learn More" — When you want to take a step further "Learn More." Sound characteristics, compatible genres, and practical setting examples all on one page. And the second page. This one is titled "Learn More About the Fulltone OCDv2," and I have packed it with sound characteristics, genres, and practical settings.
